enonce_markdown: What is the purpose of the primary key of a table in a relational database?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Every record in a table must be identifiable. The primary key is the field (or fields) whose value is different for every record.

### Solution

The primary key **uniquely identifies each record in the table** (option d). Sorting order is decided by a sort or an index, linking to another table is the role of a foreign key, and a primary key does not store the largest value.

choix.texte: It shows the order in which the records are sorted
It links a field to the primary key of another table
It stores the largest value found in the table
It uniquely identifies each record in the table

enonce_markdown:
The table STUDENT has the primary key ID.

| ID | Name | Phones |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Ada Fon | 677001122 |
| 2 | Eto Kamga | 677334455, 699112233 |

Why is this table NOT in First Normal Form (1NF)?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

A table is in 1NF when each field holds a single (atomic) value and there are no repeating groups. Look for a cell that holds a list.

### Solution

The record with ID 2 stores two telephone numbers in one cell, so **the Phones field holds more than one value** (option c). The table does have a primary key (a). Dependence of a non-key field on part of a key concerns 2NF (b is not the problem here), and a table does not need a foreign key to be in 1NF (d).

choix.texte: Name depends on only part of the primary key
The Phones field holds more than one value in a single record
A non-key field depends on another non-key field

enonce_markdown:
In a school in Bafoussam, a student can enrol in many courses and a course has many students. The school wants to store the students (StudentID, Name) and the courses (CourseCode, Title) in a relational database.

(a) Name the type of relationship between STUDENT and COURSE.

(b) Show how the database should be designed to store the enrolments, giving the fields and the keys of each table.
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

A many-to-many relationship cannot be stored directly in two tables. It is resolved by a third (junction) table that holds the primary keys of both tables as foreign keys.

### Solution

**(a)** It is a **many-to-many** relationship.

**(b)** Three tables are used:

- STUDENT(**StudentID**, Name), primary key StudentID.
- COURSE(**CourseCode**, Title), primary key CourseCode.
- ENROLMENT(**StudentID**, **CourseCode**), whose primary key is the combination of the two fields; StudentID is a foreign key to STUDENT and CourseCode is a foreign key to COURSE.

Each row of ENROLMENT records one student in one course. The two one-to-many relationships STUDENT to ENROLMENT and COURSE to ENROLMENT replace the many-to-many relationship.

enonce_markdown: A field must store the telephone number of a customer, written in the form +237677001122. Which data type is the most suitable?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Choose the data type from how the value is used. Numbers on which calculations are made are numeric; identifiers that may start with a symbol or zero, and are never added, are stored as text.

### Solution

A telephone number is never used in a calculation and this one begins with the sign +, which a numeric field cannot keep. The suitable type is **Text (Short Text)** (option a). A Number field would drop the + sign (and any leading zero), Currency is for amounts of money, and Date/Time is for dates and times.

enonce_markdown:
A shop keeps all its sales in one table:

| SaleNo | Date | CustomerName | Town | ItemCode | ItemName | UnitPrice | Qty |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 03/05 | Ngu Paul | Kumba | T1 | Bulb | 1500 | 4 |
| 2 | 03/05 | Ngu Paul | Kumba | T4 | Spanner | 900 | 1 |
| 3 | 04/05 | Etame Ann | Edea | T1 | Bulb | 1500 | 2 |

(a) Describe the data redundancy in this table and one problem it can cause.

(b) Split it into tables that remove the redundancy, naming the primary key and any foreign key of each table.
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Data that depends only on a customer or an item should be stored once, in its own table, and linked to the sales by a key. This removes redundancy and update anomalies.

### Solution

**(a)** The name and town of Ngu Paul are repeated in two records, and the name and price of the bulb in two records. If the price of a bulb changes, every record must be edited; if one is missed the data become inconsistent (update anomaly).

**(b)**

- CUSTOMER(**CustomerID**, CustomerName, Town): primary key CustomerID.
- ITEM(**ItemCode**, ItemName, UnitPrice): primary key ItemCode.
- SALE(**SaleNo**, Date, CustomerID, ItemCode, Qty): primary key SaleNo; CustomerID is a foreign key to CUSTOMER and ItemCode is a foreign key to ITEM.

(Here each sale line concerns one item. A CustomerID such as C1 for Ngu Paul and C2 for Etame Ann is added, because two customers may have the same name.)

enonce_markdown: The table EMPLOYEE(EmpID, Name, DeptCode, DeptName) has the single-field primary key EmpID. Every field holds one value, and DeptName is always the same for a given DeptCode. What is the highest normal form that this table satisfies?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

1NF: atomic values. 2NF: 1NF and no non-key field depends on only part of the key (only possible with a composite key). 3NF: 2NF and no non-key field depends on another non-key field (no transitive dependency).

### Solution

The values are atomic, so the table is in 1NF. The key has a single field, so no partial dependency is possible and the table is in 2NF. But DeptName depends on DeptCode, which is not the key: EmpID gives DeptCode and DeptCode gives DeptName (a transitive dependency). The table is therefore **in 2NF but not in 3NF** (option b). To reach 3NF, DEPARTMENT(DeptCode, DeptName) is made a separate table. Option d is wrong because a single-field key cannot have a partial dependency.

choix.texte: It is in 2NF but not in 3NF
It is not in 2NF, because DeptName depends on part of the primary key
